title: Carmina
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0261.stoa001.opp-lat5, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Praeterea didicit varias nova dogmata sectas, Quidquid laudavit Scythicis Anacharsis in arvis, Quidquid legifero profecit Sparta Lycurgo, Quidquid Erichtheis c Cynicorum turba volutat Gymnasiis, imitata tuos Epicure sodalcs : Quidquid nil verum statuens Academia duplex Personat, arroso quidquid sapit ungue Cleanthes, Quidquid Pythagoras, Democritus, Heraclitusque Deflevit, risit, tacuit; quodcunque Platonis Ingenium, quod in arce fuit, docet ordine terno. Quæ vel Aristoteles partitus membra loquendi, Argumenlosis dat retia syllogismis. Quidquid Anaximenes, Euclides, Archita, Zenon, Arcesilas, Chrysippus, Anaxagorasque dederunt, Socraticusque animus post f'tum in Phædone vivus Despiciens vastas tenuato in crure catenas, Cum tremeret mors ipsa rcum, ferretque venenum Pallida securo lictoris dextra magistro.
passages.english: Besides this, he learned the various sects with their new doctrines: whatever Anacharsis praised in the Scythian fields, whatever Sparta gained from Lycurgus the lawgiver, whatever the crowd of Cynics turns over in the gymnasia of Erechtheus' city, imitating your companions, Epicurus; whatever the twofold Academy, establishing nothing as true, proclaims aloud; whatever Cleanthes knows with his gnawed fingernail; whatever Pythagoras, Democritus and Heraclitus kept silent about, laughed at, wept over; whatever the genius of Plato, which was on the summit, teaches in its threefold order; or the parts of speech that Aristotle divided, [and which] give nets to argumentative syllogisms; whatever Anaximenes, Euclid, Archytas, Zeno, Arcesilaus, Chrysippus and Anaxagoras have given; and the Socratic spirit, living after death in the Phaedo, despising the huge chains on his wasted leg, when death itself trembled at the accused man, and the lictor's pale right hand brought the poison to the untroubled master.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'sodalcs' = sodales, 'Argumenlosis' = argumentosis, 'f'tum' = fatum, 'rcum' = reum; stray 'c' after 'Erichtheis' omitted as a footnote mark. The verbs 'deflevit, risit, tacuit' are taken in reverse order to Pythagoras, Democritus, Heraclitus (silence for Pythagoras, laughter for Democritus, weeping for Heraclitus); the English lists them in that matched order. The sentence beginning 'Quae vel Aristoteles' is loosely constructed; it is rendered as continuing the list.

passages.original: Sternitur Ægæon Briareus, Ephialta, Mimasque, Arctoas sueti lambere calce rotas. Enceladus patri jacuit, fratrique Typhœus, Euboicam hic rupem sustinet, hic Siculam. Hinc sese ad totam genitricem transtulit Orpheus, Et docuit chordas dicere Calliopen. Assurrexerunt Musæ sub laude Sororis, Et placuit divæ carmine plus pietas. 330 Quod si malernas laudes cantasse favori est, Nec valeo priscas aequiparare fides : Publicus hic pater est, vovi cui carmen, Avitus : Materia est major, si mihi Musa minor.
passages.english: Aegaeon Briareus is laid low, and Ephialtes and Mimas, who were used to lick the northern wheels [of the Bear] with their heels. Enceladus fell to the father, and Typhoeus to the brother; the one bears the Euboean rock, the other the Sicilian. From here Orpheus turned himself wholly to his mother, and taught his strings to sing of Calliope. The Muses rose up at the praise of their sister, and his devotion pleased the goddess more than his song. But if it wins favour to have sung a mother's praises, and I am not able to equal the ancient lyres, here is a father of the people, to whom I have vowed my song, Avitus: the subject is greater, even if my Muse is lesser.
passages.notes: 'malernas' read as maternas. 'Arctoas ... rotas' presumably the wheels of the Wain/Bear constellation, i.e. the giants were tall enough to reach the northern stars; sense uncertain. Which giant lies under which rock (Euboea, Sicily) follows the order 'hic ... hic'.

passages.original: O convivia, fabulæ, libelli, Risus, serielas, dicacitates, Occursus, comitatus unus idem ! Sen dclubra Dei colenda nobis, Sive ad pontificem gradus i rendi, Sive ad culmina Marcii Myronis, Tecta illustria seu videnda Livi : Sive ad doctiloqui Leonis ædes, Quo bis sex tabulas docente juris, Ultro Claudius Appius taceret, Claro obscurior in decemviratu. At si dicat epos, metrumque rhythmis. Flectat commaticis, tonante plectro, 413 Mordacem faciat silere Flaccum;
passages.english: O banquets, stories, little books, laughter, seriousness, witticisms, meetings, a single and same company! Whether we had to visit the shrines of God, or go to the bishop, or to the lofty house of Marcius Myro, or see the illustrious halls of Livius; or to the house of learned-tongued Leo, at whose teaching of the Twelve Tables of law Appius Claudius would of his own accord be silent, more obscure in his famous decemvirate. But if he recites epic, and bends metre into short-phrased rhythms with thundering plectrum, he would make biting Horace (Flaccus) fall silent;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'serielas' = serietas, 'Sen dclubra' = seu delubra, 'i rendi' = eundi (or ineundi). The line number '413' is omitted. Marcius Myro and Livius not further identified.
